title: Budget bars (production, dissipation, transport): what balances what?
summary: A bar chart of the terms of a transport equation, positive for sources and negative for sinks, with the leftover residual drawn as its own bar. It tests whether the budget of turbulent kinetic energy closes.

media.alt: Bar chart of normalised turbulent kinetic energy budget terms: production positive, dissipation negative, three smaller transport terms and an outlined residual bar.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What balances what?
read_the_figure.axes: x: budget terms (production, dissipation, turbulent transport, viscous diffusion, pressure diffusion, residual). y: term value normalised by the maximum production, dimensionless, from -1 to 1.25.
look_at: Which terms are positive and which negative? Production gains, dissipation loses.
Do production and dissipation nearly balance? Here 1.00 against -0.78.
How large is the residual compared with the smaller terms?
Are the terms distinguishable without colour (hatches differ)?
read_the_figure.proves: A budget in which the terms sum to zero within a small residual shows the numerical solution or the data satisfy the transport equation. It does not show which terms are right: two compensating errors give the same sum.
if_wrong: No residual bar: the reader cannot see whether it closes.
A residual as large as a physical term: the budget is not balanced and some term is missing or wrong.
Terms not normalised or on different units: the bars cannot be compared.

terms.meaning: Term by term accounting of a transport equation for one quantity at a location, summing to zero (steady) or to the rate of change.
Rate at which mean-flow energy is converted into turbulent kinetic energy, P = -<u v> dU/dy.
Rate at which turbulent kinetic energy is turned to heat by viscosity.
Terms that move energy from place to place without creating or destroying it overall.
What is left when all computed terms are summed; ideally zero, small if numerical errors are small.

remember: Budget at a point: P - eps + T + D + Pi + R = 0 (steady, homogeneous in the other directions).
Sign convention: positive adds energy, negative removes it.
Normalise by one number (here max production).
Show the residual as a bar, so closure is a visible test.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Bar height encodes the term, with sign by direction from the zero line. Colour and hatch pattern separate the kinds of term (solid teal for production, rose for dissipation, blue with different hatches for the three transport terms, an orange outlined hatch for the residual), so the figure survives greyscale. Numbers on the bar ends give the exact values.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A balance equation is a list of signed terms that must sum to zero. A bar chart on a common zero line makes that sum visible as bars above and below the line, and the biggest players are obvious. Adding the residual as one more bar turns closure from an assertion into something you can see.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What balances production? Dissipation, at -0.78 against +1.00: it removes 78 percent of what production creates. Q2: How are the other terms? Turbulent transport is -0.10, viscous diffusion +0.04, pressure diffusion -0.08, all small. Q3: What is the residual? Sum of the five terms is +0.08, so the residual is -0.08 or 8 percent of production, as large as pressure diffusion: the budget closes only approximately.

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Residual shown: the orange hatched bar is the evidence of closure. Without it a budget can be made to look closed by dropping or rescaling terms.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Normalising by production hides the absolute size, so a budget that closes at a trivially small level looks as good as one at a high level. A residual of 8 percent of production sounds small but is as large as the pressure diffusion term and bigger than viscous diffusion. A budget at one location says nothing about others; at the wall the order of the terms changes. Signs depend on convention.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the budget terms against wall distance as lines, so the changing balance is visible. A waterfall chart makes the running sum explicit. A table gives exact numbers.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Replace the bars by a waterfall that starts at production and subtracts each term in order, ending at the residual.

steps.title: Turbulent kinetic energy budget (steady, one-dimensional)
steps.note: P production, eps dissipation, T turbulent transport, D_nu viscous diffusion, Pi pressure diffusion, R residual.

steps.title: Closure check
steps.note: Compare with the smallest term you wish to interpret.

worked.title: Residual of the demonstration budget
worked.problem: Terms (normalised by max production): P = +1.00, eps = -0.78, T = -0.10, D = +0.04, Pi = -0.08. Find R and its size relative to P.

solution.text: The residual is minus that sum.

worked.answer: R = -0.08, 8 percent of production, as large as pressure diffusion.

Plot the budget against y+ for the near-wall layer and see which term takes over.

checks.q: Why is there a bar for the residual?
checks.answer: Closure is the test that the terms sum to zero; the residual bar makes it visible.

checks.q: A budget closes to 1e-3 of P but dissipation is computed by a model. What can you conclude?
checks.hint: Does the closure test constrain each term?
checks.answer: Not much: closure can be forced if the residual was folded into the modelled dissipation; the test is only meaningful when each term is computed independently.
